initial-setup.title: How to Get Started with your UNpkl router
initial-setup.lead: Models may differ individually, however this set of instructions is common to all models unless expressly indicated.

sections.title: Setting up your UNpkl Router
sections.html:
1. Unbox all contents of the package. Verify it includes your UNpkl device, a power adapter, and a network cable (and a SIM if your model uses cellular WAN).

2. Install the UNpkl app from the App Store or Play Store on your smartphone.

3. Provide upstream internet using one of these paths:

- Ethernet WAN — connect the supplied network cable to the WAN port on the router and the other end to your ISP modem LAN port (or upstream switch).

- Cellular WAN — if your unit has a SIM/data slot and an RM520 module, insert an activated SIM into the default SIM slot, then seat the tray fully. Use this path when you are not plugging into a wired ISP modem.

4. Connect the power cord to power up your UNpkl router. Wait 2–3 minutes (cellular models may take a bit longer for the first registration).

Note

Do not mix both upstreams for first boot unless your model and plan specifically support dual WAN. Pick Ethernet or the default SIM slot (RM520 units only), then continue with Wi‑Fi and app setup below.

sections.title: Connecting for the first time using the app
sections.html:
Locate the brochure that shipped with the package.

Connect to a UNpkl SSID before performing any of the following steps. The SSID and password are included in the brochure. You may scan the QR code to join the UNpkl Wi-Fi network using a smartphone.

Download the UNpkl app

Once you join a UNpkl Wi-Fi network, download the UNpkl app and follow the in-app instructions to set up the router.

It is preferable to use the app to set up the login and password (see Notes below). If you wish to use a web browser instead, continue with the next section.

sections.title: Admin registration and sign-in
sections.html:
Connect your smart devices to the UNpkl network. When the router powers up, you can join using the SSID and password supplied in the brochure. You can change the SSID and password via the app or web browser at https://doohickey.yhioe.lan:4433 or https://192.168.168.1:4433.

  1. Once connected to the UNpkl SSID, launch the UNpkl app or web browser and complete the admin user registration process to sign in to the UNpkl admin UI.
  2. After admin user registration is complete, we recommend enabling biometric authentication so you can easily access the UNpkl Admin app. This step is optional but recommended.

sections.title: Notes
sections.html:
Use alphanumeric characters without spaces for usernames and passwords. Example:

  • Username: SpongeBobSpatula
  • Password: KwNs2GLFIOo3nQG6YZ15Xk

The above is an example only. Set up using your own username and password.

Use alphanumeric characters, optionally with dashes (-) and dots (.), for SSIDs. Example:

  • SSID: My-Own-Personal-Space

To reset your password, go to the reset link in the app or web interface, enter the new password, and answer the security questions you chose during setup. If your answers are correct, the password you entered becomes the new admin password.

If you forget your password and security questions, a hard reset with the reset button will not help, since it is assumed at that point that the appliance is compromised.

We are happy to help you reset the password if you email us. We will walk you through step-by-step instructions over the phone. If things get messy, we are happy to provide a replacement.

sections.title: Browser security warning
sections.html: If you see a browser warning (Chrome shown below) when accessing the UNpkl web service, click Advanced and then Proceed to doohickey.yhioe.lan (unsafe).

callouts.title: Important
callouts.html: Connect to a UNpkl SSID before performing app setup or admin registration steps.

callouts.title: Tip
callouts.html: Use the UNpkl mobile app for first-time setup when possible. It is the easiest way to create your admin login and password.

callouts.title: Important
callouts.html: If you forget both your admin password and security question answers, a physical reset will not restore access. Contact UNpkl support for help.

search-and-command.title: Search & command
search-and-command.lead: Use **Search** in the UNpkl mobile app to control your local router with natural-language commands, ask questions about your network, and run in-app flows such as device provisioning. Commands are sent to the router as plain English phrases the firmware understands (SAC (search and command)).

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Search combines three paths:

  1. Direct commands — phrases that match the router command vocabulary are sent to the router (POST /c) immediately (after confirmation when a reboot or brief Wi‑Fi interruption is expected).
  2. AI assistant — questions, follow-ups, and complex requests are handled by the local Search AI, which plans actions and runs them on this router only (not cloud fleet mode).
  3. App flows — scan, provision, return device, and subscription phrases open dedicated in-app wizards (middleware / QR), not raw router HTTP.

You must be signed in to the local embedded router (connected to its Wi‑Fi or LAN). Cloud-only stats and multi-edge APIs are not available from local Search.

sections.title: Open Search
sections.html:
1. Open the UNpkl app while connected to your UNpkl router network.
  2. Tap Search in the navigation bar (or use the search entry point on your device).
  3. Type a command or question and submit.

Tips:

  • Ask how questions in plain English (for example, How do I forward a port?) — these route to the AI assistant instead of being sent blindly to the router.
  • Short follow-ups (yes, show passwords, the second network) stay in the AI conversation thread.
  • If a phrase is not in the app's command list but may exist on newer firmware, the app can offer to send it directly to the router after you confirm.

sections.title: How router commands work
sections.html:
Router control uses natural-language queries posted to POST /c as form field query. The SAC (search and command) engine on the device maps each phrase to an internal command hash (YH_CMD_* in firmware).

Wording matters — use the same verbs and structure as the examples below. Hostnames (for example Mac) must match DHCP lease names on your router.

Allow vs unblock: On port-access phrases, allow and unblock are synonyms. User intent to deny, stop, or block port access maps to block access to port …, not informal "stop" wording in the SAC command grammar.

Read-only HTTP (no /c phrase): topology, live devices, history, policy tables, wireless config snapshot, cloud status, upgrade check — the AI uses dedicated GET routes when answering questions.

sections.title: Block and unblock
sections.html:
Block destinations (websites, domains, apps) or specific source → destination pairs. Timed blocks use explicit units: minutes, hours, or days.

Examples:

  • block somewebsite.com
  • block somewebsite.com for 2 hours
  • block source iPhone from destination social.example.com
  • block source from destination from time 9 pm to time 5 pm weekdays
  • block access to port 22
  • block access to port 443 from 192.168.1.10
  • unblock somewebsite.com
  • unblock source from destination
  • unblock access to port
  • unblock access to port only from 192.168.1.10

Schedules — combine source/destination with time windows and weekdays, weekends, or everyday (for example, block source iPhone from destination social.example.com from time 9 pm to time 5 pm weekdays).

Block everything: block all / unblock all.

sections.title: Tag, assign, and rename devices
sections.html:
Organize clients and destinations with tags and groups, or rename a source for easier Search.

Examples:

  • tag destination news.example.com as News
  • tag source iPhone as Kids
  • untag destination news.example.com as News
  • untag source iPhone as Kids
  • assign source iPhone to Kids
  • unassign source iPhone
  • rename source iPhone as Johns-iPhone

sections.title: Port forwarding and firewall access
sections.html:
Port forwarding (DNAT) — expose a LAN service on a WAN port. Targets can be an IP, host:port, or a DHCP hostname.

  • forward port 22 to 192.168.168.10:2622
  • forward port 44433 to Mac
  • forward port 80 to 192.168.168.1:2222
  • forward port to unblock traffic only from 192.168.1.5
  • unforward port 443
  • unforward port from 192.168.1.10

Firewall / port access — block or allow traffic to router services by port and optional source IP list.

  • clear access to port 443
  • clear port 80
  • stop access to port 443
  • stop access to port from 10.0.0.5

Related phrases: clear access to port …, clear port …, unblock access to port only from …, unforward port … from ….

sections.title: Wi‑Fi networks
sections.html:
Manage SSIDs, passwords, VLAN IDs, and network count on 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, or both bands.

Examples:

  • set 3 wifi networks on 5ghz band
  • set 2 wifi networks on 2ghz band
  • set 3 wifi networks on both bands
  • add wifi network GuestNet with password secret123 on 5ghz band
  • delete wifi network on the 5ghz band
  • delete wifi network on the 2ghz band
  • change wifi setting psk for UNpkl-5LG-AP-1 to newwifipassword
  • change wifi setting ssid for UNpkl-5LG-AP-1 to MyWifiSSID
  • change wifi setting vlan id for UNpkl-5LG-AP-1 to 100

Add a network: add wifi network <ssid> with password <psk> on <band> band — password must be at least 8 characters, letters and digits only (no spaces or symbols). Default band is 5 GHz if omitted.

Changing an existing SSID (change wifi setting psk|ssid|hidden|vlan …) applies without reboot but may briefly disconnect clients.

Adding networks, changing network count, or deleting SSIDs requires a router reboot to take effect. The app prompts before rebooting.

Wi‑Fi join QR: Ask the AI for a scannable QR (for example, show qr code for wifi on 5ghz). Passphrases are only included after you explicitly confirm.

sections.title: Mesh and EasyMesh
sections.html:
Control mesh controller and agent roles on supported hardware.

Examples:

  • turn mesh on
  • turn agent on
  • turn controller on
  • turn mesh controller on

sections.title: WAN, LAN, and device properties
sections.html:
Configure static WAN addressing or LAN subnet.

Examples:

  • add static wan ip 10.0.0.2 gateway 10.0.0.1 dns 8.8.8.8
  • unset static wan
  • set lan to 10.0.0.1/24
  • set device property floor as 2

Other supported phrases include refresh web certificate, set device property … as …, and clear all.

sections.title: Upgrade, reboot, and logging
sections.html:
Firmware: upgrade check, force upgrade, upgrade test, upgrade test check.

Reboot: Confirm before rebooting — you will be logged out. Required after some Wi‑Fi/WAN changes.

Logging:

  • start logging
  • stop logging
  • start logging to file

Ask the AI is cloud connected? or cloud status to read cloud registration without a /c command.

sections.title: Device scan, provisioning, and subscriptions
sections.html:
These phrases open in-app flows (QR scanner, confirmations, middleware) — they are not sent as POST /c router commands.

Scan / add / provision: scan, scan device, scan new device, scan multiple devices, provision, add device

Return / remove: unprovision, unprovision device, return device, remove device

Subscription billing: pause subscription, cancel subscription, sync subscription, resume subscription

Use Search with one of the phrases above; follow on-screen steps.

sections.title: AI assistant capabilities
sections.html:
When your input is a question or needs multiple steps, local Search AI:

  1. Plans using router context (topology, live devices, network stats).
  2. Runs allowed router actions on this device only.
  3. Summarizes results in plain language (without exposing internal action names).

Supported router actions (30): execute_command, get_topology, get_platform_id, get_sysinfo, get_history, get_live, check_upgrade, force_upgrade, reboot, exec, … and execute_command for any other SAC command phrase.

Destructive shell commands via exec are blocked unless explicitly allowed. Wi‑Fi passwords require your confirmation before the AI displays them.

sections.title: SAC phrase templates
sections.html:
The firmware matcher accepts 194 SAC phrase templates (source file unsac_commands.txt in firmware). Samples by leading verb:

unblock — unblock, unblock source, unblock source from destination, unblock source from destination from time pm to time pm, unblock source from destination from time pm to time am, unblock source from destination from time am to time pm, unblock source from destination from time am to time am, unblock source from destination from time am to time

- _34 additional unblock templates in firmware_

block — block, block source, block source from destination, block source from destination from time pm to time pm, block source from destination from time pm to time am, block source from destination from time am to time pm, block source from destination from time am to time am, block source from destination from time am to time

- _33 additional block templates in firmware_

add — add wifi network, add wifi network with password, add wifi network with password ssid, add wifi network with ssid, add wifi network with ssid password, add wifi network with ssid password on, add wifi network with ssid password on band, add wifi ssid

- _7 additional add templates in firmware_

set — set lan to, set, set n wifi networks on, set n wifi networks, set device property as, set device property, set n wifi, set n wifi networks on the

- _3 additional set templates in firmware_

change — change wifi setting password for, change wifi setting password for to, change wifi setting psk for, change wifi setting psk for to, change wifi setting ssid for, change wifi setting vlan for, change wifi setting vlan for to, change wifi setting vlan id for

- _2 additional change templates in firmware_

turn — turn mesh controller on, turn controller mesh on, turn controller on, turn agent mesh on, turn mesh agent on, turn agent on, turn mesh on, turn

tag — tag source as srcgroup, tag destination as dsttag, tag source as, tag destination as, tag, tag source, tag destination

untag — untag source as srcgroup, untag destination as dsttag, untag source as, untag destination as, untag, untag source, untag destination

forward — forward port to port, forward port to, forward port, forward port to port unblock traffic only from, forward port to unblock access only from, forward port to unblock traffic only from

upgrade — upgrade, upgrade test, upgrade test check, upgrade check, upgrade force

assign — assign source to srcgroup, assign source, assign source to, assign

clear — clear all, clear, clear access to port, clear port

Placeholders such as source, destination, time, n, and port stand in for your values. See Block and unblock and Wi‑Fi networks for filled-in examples.

sections.title: Firmware command hashes
sections.html:
Each accepted phrase resolves to a YH_CMD_* hash in yh_unsac_hashes.h (194 definitions). Examples:

  • block source from destination
  • unblock source from destination
  • block source from destination from time pm to time pm
  • unblock source from destination from time pm to time pm
  • block source from destination from time pm to time am
  • unblock source from destination from time pm to time am

The app and docs stay aligned with firmware sources (yh_unsac_hashes.h, unsac_commands.txt) when commands are added or renamed. Those filenames use the internal UNSAC name; documentation refers to the feature as SAC (search and command).

sections.title: Confirmations and errors
sections.html:
Reboot prompt — After add wifi network, set N wifi networks, delete wifi network, or static WAN changes, reply yes / now to reboot immediately, later / no to apply without rebooting now, or cancel to abort.

Wi‑Fi setting changes — change wifi setting … may interrupt connections briefly; no reboot required.

Invalid command — Router may return invalid command or uh oh in the response message even with HTTP 200.

Direct send — Unknown phrases can still be tried on the router if you confirm when prompted.

settings-and-charts.title: Settings & charts
settings-and-charts.lead: Use the **Settings** and **Charts** tabs in the UNpkl mobile app to configure your router, manage AI for Search, and review network activity over time.

sections.title: Overview
sections.html: The bottom navigation includes Settings (device configuration, AI, and network actions) and Charts (historical traffic and DNS summaries). Both tabs work when you are signed in to your local UNpkl router.

sections.title: Open Settings and Charts
sections.html:
1. Open the UNpkl app while connected to your UNpkl router network.
  2. Tap Settings in the bottom bar for configuration panels.
  3. Tap Charts for network activity and DNS visualizations.

sections.title: Device settings
sections.html:
Under Device Settings on the Settings tab:

  • Enable Biometrics — turn on Face ID, Touch ID, or your device’s biometric unlock for faster sign-in to the admin app.
  • AI settings — expand to configure Search AI (see the next section). Shown for local (non-cloud) router sessions.
  • Download IP Maps Data / Delete IP Maps Data — download or remove the on-device IP geolocation database used for map and location features. Tap again to toggle between download and delete when data is present.

Cloud users also see a profile header and Cloud Management options (for example Approve Requests) above these sections.

sections.title: AI settings
sections.html:
Expand AI settings under Device Settings to control how Search uses external AI on your local router.

Disable external AI (Search) — when on, natural-language Search will not call external AI. Router SAC commands still work.

Redact sensitive data for AI — when on (recommended), Wi‑Fi passwords and similar secrets are removed from data sent to external AI. Turn off only for trusted local models on your LAN.

Assistant (Search)

By default, Search AI uses UNpkl middleware (the OpenRouter key stays on the server). Optionally set a custom OpenAI-compatible chat URL; Bearer keys are stored in the device keychain.

  • Chat completions URL — leave blank for the middleware proxy default, or enter your provider’s chat completions endpoint.
  • Model id (optional) — override the default model (placeholder shows the default OpenRouter model name).
  • API key (Bearer) — enter a Bearer token if your provider requires one, then tap Save API key. Use Clear saved key when a key is already stored and the field is empty.
  • Restore middleware defaults — reset the endpoint, model, and saved key to UNpkl middleware defaults.

For command examples and Search behavior, see Search & command.

sections.title: Network management
sections.html:
The Network Management section on Settings includes:

  • Wireless — open Wi‑Fi SSID, password, and radio settings for your UNpkl network.
  • SSH — view or paste an SSH public key, enable password authentication, and set an SSH password. Tap Save Settings to apply.
  • Upgrade Firmware — check for and install firmware updates from UNpkl. Confirm when prompted; the device may reboot.
  • Reboot Device — restart the router. Active connections will drop briefly.

Account Actions at the bottom of Settings includes Log Out.

sections.title: Charts
sections.html:
Open the Charts tab to review historical data from your router.

At the top, use the device filter to view all devices or focus on one client.

Network Activity — line chart of active connections over time, with Current Window and Connections/sec summary cards below the graph.

DNS Query Distribution — donut chart of DNS lookups by domain, with a legend showing each hostname, its share of queries, and the query count.

Charts complement Live data (real-time flows) and Search queries about traffic history. Use Charts for trends; use Live data to inspect individual connections as they happen.

callouts.title: Tip
callouts.html: Apply firmware upgrades and reboots during a maintenance window. Wireless and SSH changes can briefly interrupt connections.

live-data.title: Live data
live-data.lead: Use the **Live Data**, **Topology**, and **Maps** views in the UNpkl mobile app to watch network activity as it happens, see how devices connect, and explore where traffic goes.

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
The Live Data tab in the bottom navigation is your real-time monitoring home. It has two sub-tabs:

  • Live Data — a scrolling list of devices and their recent destinations (websites, DNS names, and connections).
  • Topology — a diagram of your network: internet gateway, UNpkl router(s), mesh agents, and connected clients.

The separate Maps tab plots live traffic on a world map when location data is available.

sections.title: Open Live Data
sections.html:
1. Open the UNpkl app while signed in to your UNpkl router (or cloud account).
  2. Tap Live Data in the bottom navigation.
  3. Use the Live Data or Topology sub-tab at the top of the screen.

The header also includes:

  • Search (magnifying glass) — open Search to run commands or ask questions about your network.
  • Play / Pause — start or stop live updates for both the device list and topology.

If data is still loading, wait a few seconds. The app retries automatically when the connection returns.

sections.title: Live Data list
sections.html:
The Live Data sub-tab groups activity by device on your network.

Each device card shows:

  • Hostname — the name your router knows for the client (from DHCP or your own rename in Search).
  • IP address and MAC address
  • Recent destinations — up to five of the latest sites or services that device contacted, with timestamps and repeat counts when the same name appears often.

Devices with recent activity are highlighted with a green edge. Devices with no recent traffic appear dimmer.

Tap the arrow on a device card to open the full destination list for that client.

A summary bar above the list shows how many devices are visible and how many live updates have been received.

sections.title: DNS only
sections.html:
Turn DNS only on to hide destination rows that are plain IP addresses and show DNS hostnames instead. This makes the list easier to read when you care about site names rather than raw IPs.

Turn DNS only off to see every destination name, including IP literals.

sections.title: Topology
sections.html:
Switch to the Topology sub-tab to see a map of how your network is wired together.

Typical nodes include:

  • Internet — your upstream connection
  • Controller — the main UNpkl router
  • Agent — mesh Wi‑Fi access points (EasyMesh setups)
  • Device — phones, laptops, and other clients

Explore the diagram:

  • Pinch or use zoom controls to magnify dense areas.
  • Drag the canvas to pan around.
  • Drag individual nodes to rearrange them; positions are remembered on your phone.

Tap a node to open details. For client devices you can:

  • Show Policy — view tags, blocks, and policy matches applied to that device.
  • Block Device / Unblock Device — quickly stop or restore network access for that client.

If topology refresh is temporarily unavailable, the app may show the last successful snapshot with a time hint until new data arrives.

From Search, when the assistant finds a device you can tap Open in Topology to jump here and highlight that client (nothing opens automatically—you choose when to navigate).

For mesh layout and hardware placement, see UNpkl EasyMesh.

sections.title: Maps
sections.html:
Tap Maps in the bottom navigation to see live traffic on a world map.

First-time setup: the map uses an on-device IP location database. Download it once from Settings → Download IP Maps Data (see Settings & charts). When the database is installed, return to Maps to see pins.

While the Maps tab is open, live records from your router feed the map. A banner shows how many live records and map pins are active.

  • Local router — pins are placed by country (or region) from the GeoIP database. Private LAN addresses appear under Local or unknown IP.
  • Cloud — pins reflect geolocated flows from your cloud-connected edges.

Tap a pin or country cluster to zoom in and, when available, see which devices and destinations contributed to that region.

The number of map pins can be lower than the live record count when many flows share the same location or IP.

sections.title: Troubleshooting tips
sections.html:
• No devices yet — confirm you are on the UNpkl Wi‑Fi or LAN and signed in. Tap play if the stream was paused.
  • Empty map — download IP Maps Data in Settings, then reopen Maps.
  • Topology empty — wait for the first refresh, or check that the router is online. Pause and play once to retry.

For broader connection issues, see Troubleshooting.

callouts.title: Tip
callouts.html: Tap the pause icon in the header to freeze updates while you read a row or explore the topology. Tap play to resume the live stream.

unpkl-saas.title: UNpkl SaaS
unpkl-saas.lead: End-to-end deployment for the UNpkl Gateway system: hardware and mesh setup, enterprise subscription, cloud provisioning, and live monitoring from the UNpkl app.

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
This guide walks through the full enterprise workflow—from acquiring gateways and access points to enrolling a subscription, linking hardware to your account, and viewing live data in the dashboard.

The five steps below follow the order most customers use:

  1. Hardware acquisition — purchase and rack UNpkl gateways.
  2. Mesh infrastructure — install APs and secure mesh backhaul.
  3. Subscription enrollment — create an account and choose a plan.
  4. Cloud provisioning — scan each controller and link it to your subscription.
  5. Live monitoring — confirm the gateway is streaming metrics to the cloud.

sections.title: Step 1: Hardware acquisition
sections.html:
Customers purchase UNpkl Gateways in bulk for high-capacity enterprise environments.

Hardware specs:

  • Chipset — mt7988-based platforms built for throughput and policy enforcement at the edge.
  • WAN connectivity — fiber optic, Ethernet, and 5G options depending on site requirements.
  • Controller role — every gateway ships pre-configured during manufacturing to act as the central network controller for its site.

Install controllers where they have reliable upstream WAN access and a clear path to mesh APs on your LAN or PoE plant.

sections.title: Step 2: Mesh infrastructure and AP installation
sections.html:
Expand coverage with AP103 access points (or compatible UNpkl mesh agents) so Wi‑Fi reaches the full floor plan.

Connectivity — connect APs to a smart PoE switch so power and data ride on the same cable run.

Mesh security — each unit joins the deployment as a mesh agent. Every mesh link uses a unique SAE secret for the backhaul so neighbor networks cannot join your mesh accidentally.

For placement, radio planning, and agent roles, see UNpkl EasyMesh.

sections.title: Step 3: Enterprise subscription enrollment
sections.html:
Before provisioning hardware, activate a UNpkl service plan tied to your organization.

  1. Choose a pricing plan that matches your gateway count and support tier.
  2. Sign up using the UNpkl iOS app, Android app, or web client.
  3. Verify your email when prompted so account recovery and billing notices reach the right inbox.
  4. Select and confirm your plan — billing and subscription management stay in the same apps going forward.

You can return to the app or web client later to update payment details or change plans.

sections.title: Step 4: Cloud provisioning and QR scanning
sections.html:
Associate each controller with your account using Search in the UNpkl app.

  1. Open Search (from the Live Data header or your app’s search entry point).
  2. Enter the command Scan device (or tap the scan suggestion when shown).
  3. Scan the QR code included in each controller package when the camera opens.
  4. Wait for confirmation — the gateway links to your email and active subscription.

Cloud endpoint — after a successful scan, the cloud assigns the device to the nearest geographical data endpoint for your region (for example https://ukeast-01.unpkl.io:44433). The gateway uses that endpoint for ongoing sync; you do not need to pick the URL manually.

Repeat the scan step for every controller in the deployment. Mesh agents discovered by an already-provisioned controller appear in topology without a separate QR scan.

For remote fleet management after provisioning, see UNpkl Cloud.

sections.title: Step 5: Live monitoring and data reporting
sections.html:
Once provisioning finishes, the Wi‑Fi controller enters its monitoring phase.

Automated sync — the gateway periodically checks the cloud for its assigned endpoint and credentials.

Live stream — when the endpoint is reachable, the controller sends live data, network metrics, and device health to your UNpkl dashboard.

In the mobile app:

  • Open Live Data for per-device traffic and topology.
  • Open Maps for geolocated flows (cloud deployments show server-side geolocation).
  • Open Charts for trends over time.

If the stream does not appear within a few minutes, confirm WAN connectivity on the gateway, that subscription status is active, and that provisioning completed for that unit. See Live data and Troubleshooting for more help.

callouts.title: Tip
callouts.html: Complete subscription enrollment (Step 3) before scanning devices (Step 4). The cloud assigns each gateway to your account and nearest regional endpoint only after both are in place.

unpkl-cloud.title: UNpkl Cloud
unpkl-cloud.lead: Manage your provisioned UNpkl gateways from the **Partner Portal** and mobile app—live traffic, maps, topology, security logs, and automation in one place.

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
UNpkl Cloud is the online control plane for gateways you have subscribed and provisioned (see UNpkl SaaS). Once a controller is linked to your account, it sends live network data to the nearest regional cloud endpoint. You sign in to the portal or app to see what is happening across your sites.

The cloud keeps your account, devices, subscriptions, and audit history together. UNpkl middleware sits between the portal, mobile app, and cloud services—it handles sign-in, routes requests to the right regional endpoint, and powers features such as the cloud AI assistant using your organization context.

At a glance, UNpkl Cloud helps you:

  • See which networks are online and whether anything needs attention
  • Watch live device activity, maps, topology, and connection trends
  • Review what was blocked and why (ads, trackers, malicious destinations, or your own rules)
  • Describe monitoring or automation jobs in plain language

sections.title: Sign in to the Partner Portal
sections.html:
Open the UNpkl Partner Portal in a web browser and sign in with the same email you used for subscription enrollment.

Use Account Sign up or Reset if you need to create an account or recover access. Clear Auth & Start Fresh helps when a browser session is stuck during troubleshooting.

sections.title: Home dashboard
sections.html:
After sign-in, the Home tab shows a summary of your organization—the Network Operations Command Center.

Need Attention — alerts and jobs that may require a follow-up (for example pending approvals or failed tasks).

Networks — how many gateways are registered and online, with a quick security status.

Jobs — scheduled or custom monitoring and automation tasks running on your edges.

Metrics — recorded measurements from those jobs (bandwidth, health checks, and similar).

Audit logs — a preview of recent blocklist and policy events from your gateways; open the full audit view for details.

Use the top navigation to move between Home, Subscription, Live, and Jobs.

sections.title: Live monitoring
sections.html:
The Live tab combines four views on one screen so you can monitor activity without switching tools.

Live — devices on your networks and their recent destinations (websites and DNS names). Toggle DNS only to hide plain IP addresses and focus on site names. This mirrors what you see in the mobile app’s Live data tab, aggregated for cloud fleets.

Maps — where traffic is going geographically. Markers show countries and regions your devices contact; useful for multi-site or roaming deployments.

Topology — how gateways, mesh agents, and clients connect back to the internet. Search by hostname, MAC, or IP to find a device quickly.

Connections — a live chart of active connections per gateway (hostname), so you can spot spikes or drops over time.

The mobile app offers the same live views when signed in with your cloud account. See Live data for app-specific tips.

sections.title: Security and audit logs
sections.html:
UNpkl Cloud applies layered protection on your gateways: known malicious addresses, category blocklists, and optional custom rules you upload for your organization. When traffic is stopped, an audit entry records what happened.

Open Live → Audit logs to inspect events by device.

Columns mean:

  • Time — when the event occurred
  • Source — the device that made the request (internal IP)
  • Target — the site or service it tried to reach
  • Action — typically block when a rule matched
  • Match / command — why it matched (for example an exact DNS block)

Custom allow lists can override system blocks when you need a trusted partner or internal service to stay reachable. Organization administrators manage those rules from the portal or API.

sections.title: AI assistant
sections.html:
The AI assistant (bottom-right in the portal) helps you work in plain English instead of memorizing menus. It can use your subscription and device context when you ask about networks, jobs, maps, or security.

Examples of what you can ask:

  • Chart WAN bandwidth on a schedule
  • Summarize which devices generated the most blocks today
  • Open the job catalog for a pre-built monitoring template

Press Enter to send a message; Shift+Enter adds a new line. Use Attach when you need to include a file with your request.

Cloud Search in the mobile app follows a similar idea for fleet operators; local router Search is documented under Search & command.

sections.title: How cloud and middleware fit together
sections.html:
You do not need to pick a regional server URL yourself. After provisioning, each gateway learns its assigned endpoint (for example a host like ukeast-01.unpkl.io) and streams data there automatically.

  • Gateway — enforces policy on your LAN and sends live metrics and audit events upstream
  • Cloud — stores accounts, devices, subscriptions, statistics, and audit history
  • Middleware — connects the portal and app to cloud services, including cloud AI chat
  • Partner Portal — web dashboard for fleet overview, live views, jobs, and audit logs
  • Mobile app — Live data, maps, topology, charts, and Search when signed in as a cloud user

If live data is missing, confirm the gateway is online, provisioning completed, and your subscription is active. See UNpkl SaaS for enrollment and scanning steps, and Troubleshooting for connection help.

callouts.title: Tip
callouts.html: Complete subscription enrollment and device provisioning before using the portal. Gateways must be linked to your account before live data appears here or in the mobile app.

unpkl-easymesh.title: UNpkl EasyMesh
unpkl-easymesh.lead: Extend Wi‑Fi coverage across your home or office with UNpkl **EasyMesh**—one shared network name, secure mesh backhaul, and automatic routing to the main gateway (**controller**).

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
EasyMesh is relevant when you add UNpkl Wi‑Fi access points that should work as agents (mesh extenders) under a single controller gateway.

In plain terms, an EasyMesh agent is a Wi‑Fi extender with stronger security than a typical repeater: agents discover the controller automatically, use encrypted backhaul links, and inherit Wi‑Fi settings from the controller once paired.

Typical layout:

  • Controller — the UNpkl gateway connected to your ISP (WAN). It runs policy, DHCP, and cloud sync.
  • Agent(s) — ceiling‑mount or PoE access points that extend coverage. Clients roam between controller and agents on the same SSIDs.

Common sizes:

  • 1 controller + 1 agent
  • 1 controller + 2 agents (common retail mesh package)
  • 1 controller + 3 or more agents for larger floors

Enterprise deployments often use a UNpkl Gateway controller, a PoE switch, and multiple AP103 (or compatible) ceiling agents—see UNpkl SaaS for that workflow.

sections.title: Controller and agent roles
sections.html:
Every UNpkl unit can act as either:

  • Controller — main router on your WAN link; owns the mesh and customer Wi‑Fi networks
  • Agent — extends Wi‑Fi; connects to the controller over wired LAN or a private backhaul SSID

turn agent on sets the device role to agent and turns it into a wireless switch: it bridges client Wi‑Fi while the controller remains the gateway.

There are two ways to add an agent. Prefer Option 1 (wired LAN) when you can temporarily cable the units together—backhaul settings sync automatically. Use Option 2 when the agent must join over Wi‑Fi only (you copy the controller’s backhaul SSID and PSK onto the agent first).

UNpkl configures controllers at the factory with turn controller on, so you usually do not need to change the controller role yourself.

sections.title: What you need
sections.html:
Buy two or more UNpkl Wi‑Fi access points when you want mesh coverage (one gateway plus at least one agent).

Access points are available from the UNpkl store or authorized retailers. For permanent wired backhaul to agents, use a PoE switch so power and data share one cable run to ceiling mounts.

You will need:

  • The controller (gateway already on your WAN / ISP)
  • The UNpkl mobile app or local web UI with Search
  • For Option 1: an Ethernet cable between the agent’s LAN port and the controller’s LAN port (temporary for sync, or leave it for wired backhaul)
  • For Option 2: the controller brochure and each agent brochure (factory backhaul SSID and PSK)

sections.title: Set up the controller
sections.html:
1. Complete Initial setup on the gateway that will be your controller (WAN, admin login, Wi‑Fi).
  2. Confirm it has internet access and that you can open Search on the app or web UI.
  3. Leave the device in controller role (factory default).

If you are unsure, open Live data → Topology after agents join—you should see the controller at the top of the mesh tree.

sections.title: Set up an agent
sections.html:
Configure one agent at a time. UNpkl units ship as controllers; the steps below convert an extra unit into an agent under your main gateway.

Option 1 — Wired LAN (recommended)

Easiest path: convert the unit to an agent, then let the controller push backhaul settings over Ethernet.

  1. Connect your phone or laptop to the unit that will become the agent (not the main gateway). Join that unit’s Wi‑Fi or plug Ethernet into its LAN port, then open the UNpkl app.
  2. Open Search and run: turn agent on

The device reboots and becomes an agent (wireless switch role).

  1. Connect an Ethernet cable from the agent’s LAN port to a LAN port on the controller.

After that link is up, backhaul settings sync automatically from the controller to the agent. You do not need to copy backhaul SSID or PSK by hand.

Leave the cable connected for wired backhaul, or unplug after sync if you want the agent to use Wi‑Fi backhaul later (confirm the agent still appears under the controller in Topology).

Important

After turn agent on, the unit cannot be switched back to a controller without advanced manual steps. Make sure you ran the command on the extra device, not on your main gateway.

Option 2 — Wireless backhaul (manual credentials)

Use this when you cannot cable the agent to the controller and must join over Wi‑Fi. Retarget the agent’s factory backhaul credentials to match the controller brochure, then enable the agent role.

#### Connect to the agent

  1. Connect your laptop or phone to the agent you are configuring—preferably over Ethernet to the agent’s LAN port. If you use Wi‑Fi, be sure you joined that agent’s network, not the controller’s.
  2. Sign in to the UNpkl app or web UI on the agent.
  3. Open Search.

#### Point the agent at the controller backhaul

From the agent’s Search box, run two commands (replace placeholders with values from the brochures):

  • change wifi setting ssid for <Current Backhaul SSID> to <Controller Backhaul SSID>
  • change wifi setting psk for <Current Backhaul PSK> to <Controller Backhaul PSK>

Example (names will differ on your devices):

  • Agent brochure might show Backhaul SSID: UNpkl-AP-123456-1 and Backhaul PSK: abcdefghijklmnop
  • Controller brochure shows Backhaul SSID: UNpkl-AP-654321-1 and Backhaul PSK: qrstuvwxyz123456

Use the agent’s current SSID as the for name in both commands, and paste the controller’s SSID and PSK as the to values.

#### Enable the agent role

In Search on the agent, run: turn agent on

The device reboots, joins the controller over Wi‑Fi backhaul, and imports Wi‑Fi settings from the controller. Repeat for each additional agent.

sections.title: Verify in the app
sections.html:
After agents come online:

  1. Connect to the controller network (or sign in to your cloud account).
  2. Open Live data → Topology.
  3. Confirm Controller at the root and Agent nodes linked below it, then client devices attached.

In UNpkl Cloud, the Live tab shows the same topology and connection charts for fleet deployments.

sections.title: Placement tips
sections.html:
• Mount agents between the controller and areas with weak signal—not at the far edge of coverage.
  • Prefer line of sight where possible; avoid metal racks, concrete pillars, and microwave ovens between nodes.
  • For ceiling APs, center agents over the floor area they should serve.
  • If clients stick to one node, move the agent closer to the dead zone or add another agent mid‑path.

See Troubleshooting if roaming is poor or an agent never appears in topology.

sections.title: Mesh commands
sections.html:
Use Search on the controller or agent (while locally connected) for mesh role commands:

  • turn mesh on
  • turn agent on
  • turn controller on
  • turn mesh controller on

Full phrase lists and SAC behavior are in Search & command.

sections.title: Bulk agent setup
sections.html: If you are onboarding many agents (for example a full office rollout), contact UNpkl support—we can provide scripts to automate backhaul retargeting and turn agent on instead of stepping through the UI for each unit.

callouts.title: Tip
callouts.html: UNpkl devices ship as controllers by default. A mesh package of three may arrive with two agents and one controller already configured—skip agent pairing for those units.

callouts.title: Important
callouts.html: After the next step the unit becomes an agent and cannot be switched back to a controller without advanced manual steps. Double‑check that backhaul SSID and PSK match the controller brochure, not the agent brochure.

faq.title: FAQ
faq.lead: Quick answers to common UNpkl router, app, and Search questions.

sections.title: Router and connectivity
sections.html:
Cannot login into the app

Make sure you are connected to an SSID (Wi-Fi network) on the UNpkl router

Lost password and cannot remember security questions?

Warning

Do not attempt to do a physical reset by pressing the physical reset button here! Follow instructions below.

Locate the admin password in the packaged brochure

If you forget the admin password and the answers to your security questions, you can reset local admin data from the LAN using SSH:

Important

The commands above remove local admin data on the router. Use only when you control the device on your LAN and understand that existing admin accounts will be cleared.

If you need assistance with the above we are happy to assist - please send us a note.

Cannot access the internet?

Please make sure the router WAN cable is connected to the LAN port on your Internet Service Provider (ISP) modem (or upstream switch).

Reboot the router and try again. If the problem continues, see Troubleshooting and confirm the WAN link lights on both devices.

After reboot, register a new admin user through Initial setup. Contact UNpkl support if you need step-by-step help.

sections.title: Search and blocking
sections.html:
Block or unblock commands seem ineffective

When you enter a command like block facebook, the Wi‑Fi network learns IP addresses as DNS resolves each site and blocks them. Results can take a moment to appear in Live data.

If blocking still looks wrong, note the exact command you used and contact support.

sections.title: Mobile app
sections.html:
App stopped working — cannot log in

The most likely cause is an expired web certificate on the router.

We try to renew certificates automatically. To restore app access quickly:

  1. Open the router web interface in a browser and accept the self-signed certificate warning so you can sign in.
  2. In Search, run upgrade to install the latest build and certificates.

When the upgrade finishes, sign in again from the iOS or Android app.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.lead: Steps to diagnose connectivity, Wi‑Fi mesh, cloud sync, and advanced issues on UNpkl routers and access points.

sections.title: No internet
sections.html:
1. Confirm the WAN cable is plugged into the UNpkl gateway and the LAN port on your ISP modem (or upstream switch).
  2. Check link lights on both the modem and UNpkl WAN port.
  3. Power-cycle the ISP modem, wait two minutes, then reboot the UNpkl device.
  4. Open Live data and look for blocked DNS, policy blocks, or unusual traffic that might explain a partial outage.
  5. If the router was recently reset, complete Initial setup again and register a new admin user.

See FAQ if you cannot sign in to the app or need to recover an admin password.

sections.title: App and login issues
sections.html:
Cannot connect to the router in the app

Join a UNpkl Wi‑Fi SSID (or connect over Ethernet to the device LAN) before opening the app. Credentials are in the brochure shipped with the unit.

Certificate or login failures

An expired web certificate is the most common cause of sudden app login failures.

  1. Open the router web UI in a browser and accept the self-signed certificate warning if prompted.
  2. In Search, run upgrade to install the latest build and renewed certificates.
  3. Sign in again from the iOS or Android app.

sections.title: Wi‑Fi and EasyMesh
sections.html:
Mesh extends coverage through a controller (main gateway) and agent nodes. When clients stick to the wrong node or speeds collapse on an agent, check signal strength first—not just “bars” on the phone.

Open Live data → Topology in the UNpkl app. Each agent and client (STA) shows RSSI in dBm (a negative number, for example -58 dBm).

Signal strength quick reference (dBm)

-30 to -50 dBm — Excellent. Ideal for streaming, gaming, and agent backhaul. -60 to -65 dBm — Good. Reliable for everyday use. -67 dBm — Common roaming threshold; many phones start looking for a closer node around here. -75 to -85 dBm — Weak. Expect packet loss, latency, and dropped calls. Below -80 dBm — Poor. Reposition agents or move the client closer before tuning software settings.

For mesh setup (backhaul SSID/PSK, turn agent on, placement), see UNpkl EasyMesh.

Devices won't roam (“sticky” clients)

Symptom: You move near another node but the phone stays on a distant one with RSSI around -80 dBm or worse.

  1. Toggle Wi‑Fi off and on on the device to force a fresh scan.
  2. In Topology, confirm the closer agent shows stronger dBm (for example -55 dBm vs -78 dBm on the current link).
  3. Reposition agents: nodes that are too close can both read -65 dBm or better, so hysteresis keeps the phone on the old node—spread them further apart.

Slow speeds on an agent

Symptom: Clients on the controller are fast; clients on an agent are slow despite “good” RSSI to the agent.

  1. In Topology, check backhaul RSSI between controller and agent—not just client-to-agent signal.
  2. If backhaul is below -70 dBm or flagged poor, move the agent closer to the controller or reduce obstacles (concrete, metal, microwave ovens).
  3. Prefer Ethernet backhaul to the agent when possible; it frees wireless bands for clients.

Drops and latency

  1. Avoid long daisy chains (Router → Agent 1 → Agent 2 → Agent 3) unless your layout requires it; prefer agents linking back toward the controller.
  2. Run Optimize network / channel scan in the app if available, or reduce interference from neighboring Wi‑Fi on the same channel.

sections.title: Cloud offline
sections.html:
1. Confirm the gateway has working internet (WAN checks above).
  2. Verify DNS and NTP can reach the internet—cloud registration depends on both.
  3. Open Settings → Cloud and re-enter your organization code if registration expired or the device was replaced.
  4. Check Live data on the device locally; if local admin works but cloud does not, note the cloud status shown in Settings before contacting support.

sections.title: Developers and SSH
sections.html:
For developers familiar with OpenWrt-style tooling, you can SSH to the router using credentials from the shipped brochure (hostname is often doohickey.yhioe.lan on the LAN).

UNpkl’s main userspace process is yhioe—it handles most wireless, policy, and SAC behavior. Useful starting points:

UNpkl uses nftables (not legacy iptables) for filtering. You should see nftables kernel modules only on this platform:

The yhq / yhq6 tables are a good place to inspect IPv4/IPv6 policy state.

Custom development

If you are extending nftables policy or integrating with yhioe, send us a note—we are happy to assist with platform-specific details.

sections.title: Get help
sections.html:
Before opening a ticket:

  1. Note your firmware version from Settings or after running upgrade in Search.
  2. Export or screenshot Live data → Topology when the issue involves mesh or signal strength—include dBm values for affected clients and agents.
  3. Collect diagnostics from Settings → Support if your build exposes that option.
  4. For password recovery or SSH reset workflows, see FAQ.

zero-trust.title: Zero Trust on UNpkl
zero-trust.lead: Deny all until you allow—on your UNpkl router, with plain-language Search commands.

sections.title: What Zero Trust means here
sections.html:
By default, Zero Trust needs no subscription. Deny-all, allow lists, user groups, and intranet rules all run on the router itself.

If you subscribe, UNpkl Cloud allows destinations only when they are not blacklisted by TALOS and other threat-intelligence feeds, and you can add a custom CSV via AI to harden the network further.

On most home routers, the default is allow all: every device can reach the internet until you block something.

Zero Trust flips that: deny all until a destination (or device → destination) is explicitly allowed. Traffic that is not on your allow list is blocked at the edge—whether that edge faces the internet or your intranet (LAN, SD‑WAN, or other private prefixes).

UNpkl makes that switch practical. You do not need enterprise policy UIs—you change the default in Search, then unblock what your household or office needs. The same grouping model also supports zone-style / VRF-like policy: put sources into users or tags, then allow only specific destination networks.

sections.title: Turn on deny-all
sections.html:
Change the default policy from allow-all to deny-all with one command:

  • block all

On the latest builds, you can also use:

  • deny all

Both set the network default so new destinations are blocked until you allow them.

Important

After block all / deny all, apps and websites stop working until you unblock what you need. Start with a short allow list (for example DNS-friendly sites you use every day), then expand as you watch Live data.

To return to a normal allow-all default:

  • unblock all

sections.title: Allow what you need
sections.html:
Once deny-all is on, unblock destinations by name:

  • unblock google
  • unblock github

You can combine steps in one Search submission:

  • block all. unblock google and github

That turns on Zero Trust and immediately allows Google and GitHub in a single phrase.

Unblock more sites the same way as you discover what is missing (mail, school portals, streaming, and so on). Check Live data to see which destinations devices are trying to reach.

sections.title: Per-device exceptions
sections.html:
Zero Trust is not only “whole network allow lists.” You can selectively allow one device to reach certain destinations—or categories—without opening them for everyone.

Examples:

  • unblock tims-iPhone from math websites
  • unblock tims-iPhone from math websites for 2 hours

Use the hostname the router shows in Live data (or a name you set in Search). Timed unblocks expire automatically when the duration ends.

This is useful for homework windows, guest devices, or giving one phone access while the rest of the network stays on deny-all.

sections.title: Assign devices to a user
sections.html:
Group several devices under one user (or household member name), then apply policy to that person in one command.

First assign devices:

  • assign iPhone, Mac and RokuTV to John

Hostnames should match what Live data shows (or names you have already set). After that, John’s phones, computer, and TV share the same policy target.

Then allow temporary access for that user—for example a short window while deny-all stays on for everyone else:

  • unblock John for 10 minutes

When the timer ends, John’s devices return to the network default (deny-all if you have Zero Trust enabled).

You can still combine user and destination rules when needed (for example unblocking a person from a category of sites). Assign once; reuse the user name in later Search phrases.

sections.title: Intranet zones and power policy
sections.html:
Zero Trust is not only about the public internet. You can build intranet policy—similar in spirit to zone-based routing or VRF—by grouping sources and destinations, then allowing only the paths you choose.

Typical pattern:

  1. Assign devices to a person.
  2. Tag that person (or group) with a zone or corporate label.
  3. Unblock that group from an internal or SD‑WAN prefix.

Example:

  • assign tims-iPhone and tims-MacbookPro to Tim
  • tag Tim as FT Corporate
  • unblock FT Corporate from 10.10.0.0/16

That places Tim in the FT Corporate group and allows those devices to reach the internal (or SD‑WAN) 10.10.0.0/16 network. Other devices stay on the default deny-all (or your other rules) and do not get that internal route access unless you allow them the same way.

Use this for home-office split networks, guest isolation, or giving a work profile access to a private CIDR without opening it to every client on the LAN.

sections.title: Suggested workflow
sections.html:
1. Open Search on the UNpkl app while connected to the router.
  2. Run block all (or deny all on the latest build).
  3. Unblock essentials: for example unblock google and github (or combine with step 2 as block all. unblock google and github).
  4. Optionally assign household devices to users (for example assign iPhone, Mac and RokuTV to John).
  5. For intranet / SD‑WAN access, tag users into zones and unblock those groups from private prefixes (for example tag Tim as FT Corporate then unblock FT Corporate from 10.10.0.0/16).
  6. Watch Live data for blocked attempts; unblock sites, devices, users, or zones as needed.
  7. Use timed access such as unblock John for 10 minutes when only a short window is required.

When you no longer want deny-all as the default, run unblock all and refine with normal block / unblock rules instead.

sections.title: Related commands
sections.html:
• Deny all by default — block all or deny all
  • Restore allow-all default — unblock all
  • Allow a site — unblock google
  • Deny-all + allow list in one go — block all. unblock google and github
  • Device → destination — unblock tims-iPhone from math websites
  • Timed device access — unblock tims-iPhone from math websites for 2 hours
  • Assign devices to a user — assign iPhone, Mac and RokuTV to John
  • Timed user access — unblock John for 10 minutes
  • Tag a user as a zone / group — tag Tim as FT Corporate
  • Allow a group to an internal prefix — unblock FT Corporate from 10.10.0.0/16

Full block/unblock grammar, schedules, and port rules are in Search & command.

callouts.title: Tip
callouts.html: Run Zero Trust commands while signed in to the local router (connected to its Wi‑Fi or LAN). See Search & command for how phrases are sent to the device.
